synthesis.headline: The summer dipole reorganizes: a Great Basin cutoff deepens the western trough and a transient Atlantic-seaboard ridge amplifies, but the durable heat stays welded to Texas and the South
synthesis.narrative:
The warm-season dipole Tlaloc has tracked for well over two weeks is still the organizing story, but today it wears a different face than yesterday's Midwest-centered ridge. The 12Z 500 mb analysis puts a deep, slightly negatively tilted trough over the central Rockies into the northern Plains, with a genuine cutoff low closed off near 588 dam and a -15C core over the Great Basin (Nevada/southwestern Utah). Downstream, the ridge has slid east and amplified over the Atlantic seaboard, reaching 594 dam over the mid-Atlantic and southeastern Canada. The result is a semi-blocked, slow-moving dipole rather than progressive flow, though the geometry is a longitudinally offset trough-ridge couplet, not the stacked high-over-low of a Rex block. The important caveat is that the eastern ridge is the transient half: WPC's medium range reasserts eastern troughing early next week as multiple shortwaves round the ridge and a closed low sets up near the Great Lakes Sunday-Monday. The durable half remains the southern-tier heat ridge and the deep Arctic/Canadian trough to its north.

The centers of action ring the pattern. At the surface, a 1011 mb low near the central Rockies trails a cold front into the southern Plains and a warm/stationary boundary east across the central Plains into the lower Missouri Valley; the tightest isobar packing there, fed by Gulf moisture pumped north on the western flank of a 1035 mb Bermuda-type high off the Southeast coast, marks the day's best convergence and supports the central Plains-to-upper Mississippi Valley severe threat (large hail over two inches the primary hazard from eastern Nebraska into Minnesota and Wisconsin). A second, weaker low over the upper Midwest/Great Lakes drags a cold front into the Ohio Valley, where upper-60s to low-70s dewpoints keep the airmass primed. The eastern focus today is the Mid-Atlantic, where a convergence zone between stationary and cold fronts sets up a heavy-rain and flash-flood corridor along I-95 with a damaging-wind and marginal tornado threat. The most dangerous and most durable element remains heat: Extreme Heat Warnings run from the Desert Southwest through the Deep South, centered on Texas, with record highs and dangerously warm overnight lows.

The upper structure ties it together. The Great Basin cutoff is separated from the westerlies and will pivot slowly rather than translate, anchoring the western trough in place, while an 80-90 kt jet streak across the northern Plains and upper Midwest provides a diffluent exit region that enhances the central Plains lift; a stronger jet near 105 kt arcs across the Northeast and Maritimes along the ridge periphery. GOES Air Mass RGB reads consistently: the broad orange-red plume over the southern Plains, Southwest and northern Mexico is ridge-related subsident dryness, not a stratospheric intrusion, while a sharper dry streamer curls cyclonically from the southern Plains northeast to the Great Lakes on the forward flank of the western trough. The crisp color gradient from the Great Lakes southwest through the Ohio Valley into the mid-South marks the implied jet corridor and airmass seam, with a white cirrus outflow shield spilling from the Ohio Valley into New England on its poleward side. On the regime question, the CPC ensemble means tell a coherent story when read against each other: the 6-10 day (Aug 25-29) shows a transient northern-tier amplification, a +9 to +12 dam ridge over interior western Canada with the zero line near the central Plains and Great Lakes; but the 8-14 day (Aug 27-Sep 2) erases that western Canadian ridge entirely, retreating the ridge core southwest to the Desert Southwest and northern Mexico (a 594 dam closed high, +3 to +6 dam) beneath a deepening Arctic trough that dominates the northern tier. That pair points to genuine geographic contraction and southwest retreat of the durable ridge rather than a rebuild in place, and WPC's days 3-7 discussion closes the loop, holding the anchoring upper high over the southern tier while shortwaves keep the East unsettled.
synthesis.climate_context: This is peak-summer North America running close to the seasonal script. The North American Monsoon is active, streaming moisture north under the Southwest ridge for high-terrain convection and the Four Corners flash-flood threat, while severe-weather season is expressed as ridge-periphery, northern-stream storms along a wavy frontal zone rather than classic deep-Plains supercells. The ENSO backdrop is a decisively developing warm state: the ONI has climbed out of last year's weak La Nina (about -0.6 in late 2025) through neutral in late winter to roughly +1.39 by MJJ 2026, a clear transition toward moderate El Nino. That configuration typically favors the East Pacific while shear and dry air suppress the Atlantic, and today's tropics fit the split as the basin nears its early-September peak: the Atlantic is quiet with no development expected in seven days, while the East and Central Pacific are busy with Hurricane Lala near Lisianski Island, a near-certain (90%) development east-southeast of Hawaii that the islands should monitor, and a tropical wave south of Mexico with high (80%) seven-day odds. Teleconnection indices are only a weak, directional cross-check in summer, but they corroborate rather than drive the height story: a strongly negative NAO (-0.90 mean, -1.28 latest) is consistent with the persistent Atlantic/eastern-seaboard blocking and cutoff tendency, while the weakly negative PNA and a volatile AO align loosely with the deepening Canadian trough and retreating Southwest ridge the height and PV fields already show.
synthesis.regional_notes: Severe weather is at outlook level this morning. In the East, SPC's Tennessee-area Severe Thunderstorm Watch 603 was already weakening on substantial overturning and was set to expire near 11Z with no replacement; attention shifts to the Mid-Atlantic, where 40-50 kt shear and favorable hodographs support a couple of tornadoes from the Delmarva into central New Jersey along the I-95 heavy-rain corridor, with another round for the Carolinas and Mid-Atlantic Friday. On the northern stream, the central Plains-upper Mississippi Valley threat features hail exceeding two inches into the early evening and continues Friday across central and eastern Nebraska. In the Southwest, monsoon convection persists over the Four Corners with localized flash-flood risk over burn scars, slot canyons and urban areas, and scattered Arizona storms with lower gust potential than the prior day. Extreme Heat Warnings blanket the Desert Southwest through the Deep South with Heat Advisories along Florida and the Southeast coast; low-80s overnight lows offer minimal relief. In Canada, the action stays at high latitudes and along the Atlantic seaboard frontal zone (tightest gradient between the Quebec-Maritimes coast and offshore lows near the Gulf of St. Lawrence), while the western provinces sit quiet under a 1028-1029 mb ridge.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary: The most prominent features on this 1200Z 20 August 2026 analysis are a sprawling Bermuda-type high centered near 1035 mb off the Southeast Atlantic coast and a 1017-1018 mb high anchored over the north-central Plains, together establishing a broad ridge axis that dominates the eastern two-thirds of the continent with a slack gradient across much of the interior. A complex of surface lows and associated frontal boundaries is the primary focus for lift: a low near the central Rockies/Colorado vicinity around 1011 mb trails a cold front southeastward into the southern Plains and a warm front or stationary boundary eastward across the central Plains into the lower Missouri Valley, with tightly packed isobars immediately ahead of that cold front suggesting enhanced low-level convergence and moisture transport from the Gulf. A second, weaker low tracks across the upper Midwest-Great Lakes region with a cold front sweeping south-southeast into the Ohio Valley, where dew points plotted in the upper 60s to low 70s °F indicate substantial moisture in place ahead of it. Along the Pacific Coast, a low near the Pacific Northwest around 1011 mb is driving a frontal boundary onshore with a tight gradient over the northern Rockies, but the maritime airmass there is comparatively cool and moisture-limited relative to the Gulf feed in the central U.S. The Atlantic high's western ridge is the principal moisture pump, channeling Gulf air northward into the frontal zone from Texas through the mid-Mississippi Valley, making that corridor the most credible focus for organized convective lift based on the surface fields shown.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This CMC surface analysis valid 0000Z Thursday 20 August 2026 shows a broad ridge of high pressure anchoring much of western Canada, with the 1028 mb centre plotted over what appears to be the BC interior or Alberta foothills and a secondary 1029 mb high over the central prairies area, producing a slack gradient and predominantly settled conditions across the western provinces. A cluster of lows and associated frontal boundaries occupies the eastern half of the domain at Canadian latitudes: a 991-992 mb low sits well into the upper portion of the chart consistent with the Arctic basin or high-latitude Baffin region, while a 998 mb low labelled NEW and another near 997 mb appear positioned over or just north of the Gulf of St. Lawrence and Atlantic Canada, with cold and warm frontal segments trailing southwestward into the northeastern United States where they connect to a 995 mb low over the interior northeast. The tightest pressure gradient visible north of the border runs along the Atlantic seaboard frontal zone, where isobar spacing narrows markedly between the Quebec-Maritimes coast and the offshore systems, implying the strongest surface winds in that corridor. Across the central and southern prairies the isobars are widely spaced between the western high and a modest 1009-1010 mb trough that tracks through the mid-continent into the US Plains, consistent with a weak late-summer disturbance with limited gradient; frontal symbology on that trough is present but the boundary appears diffuse. Southern Ontario and Quebec sit between the retreating Atlantic low complex and the continental ridge, with isobar orientation suggesting a southerly to southwesterly flow that would advect Gulf moisture northward ahead of the approaching frontal system.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: At 500 mb valid 1200 UTC 20 August 2026, the dominant longwave pattern features a deep trough centered over the central Rockies into the northern Plains, with heights falling to near 570 dam at the base, and a pronounced ridge axis extending from the Gulf Coast northeastward into the western Atlantic, with heights reaching 594 dam over the mid-Atlantic and southeastern Canada. A closed low is evident over the Great Basin, centered roughly over Nevada or southwestern Utah, with a closed 588 dam contour and a cold temperature core near -15 C; this is a genuine cutoff, separated from the main westerly flow, and its isolation implies it will pivot slowly rather than translate quickly downstream. The trough over the central and northern Rockies into the Plains has a slight negative tilt — its axis angles from northwest to southeast — which is consistent with an implied diffluent, accelerating exit region and enhanced lift across the central Plains. The shaded green regions indicate wind speeds in the 70-95 knot range, with a jet streak visible arcing across the northern Plains and upper Midwest at roughly 80-90 knots, and a separate swath of enhanced winds over the northeastern U.S. and Canadian Maritimes approaching 105 knots near the ridge axis. The overall pattern appears semi-blocked: the cutoff low anchors the western trough in place while the downstream ridge is amplified and relatively stationary, producing a slow-moving dipole rather than progressive flow, though the geometry does not meet the stacked high-over-low definition of a Rex block.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB from 1341 UTC 20 August 2026 shows a broad expanse of orange-red tones across the southern Plains, Southwest, and northern Mexico, consistent with dry upper-tropospheric air under a summer ridge rather than a stratospheric intrusion. The most prominent organized deep convection appears as a bright white cluster over the central Gulf of Mexico and a second area near the Texas-Mexico border region, with additional scattered white tops over the interior Southeast near Mississippi and Alabama. A striking airmass boundary runs from roughly the Great Lakes southwestward through the Ohio Valley and into the mid-South, where the orange-red dry air to the west transitions sharply to the green moist tropical air mass to the east and south; this boundary marks the implied jet corridor, and the green signature flooding the Southeast and Gulf Coast reflects the deep moisture of the tropical airmass. A well-defined curved dry streamer, rendered in reddish-orange tones and visually distinct from the broader ridge coloring to its south, wraps cyclonically from the southern Plains northward and then arcing northeast across the upper Midwest toward the Great Lakes, consistent with a dry intrusion on the forward and equatorward flank of a mid-latitude trough; a broad white high-cloud shield stretching from the Ohio Valley northeast into New England marks what appears to be the principal cyclone outflow on the poleward side of this same boundary.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: The polar jet and its associated airmass boundary are visible across northern Canada as a sharp transition from the blue-purple tones at high latitudes to the orange-red tones farther south, with the boundary oriented roughly west-northwest to east-northeast across the upper portion of the disk. A compact, relatively saturated reddish-orange filament extending southward from the northwestern corner of the image into the eastern Pacific, distinct from the broader warm coloring under the subtropical ridge, is consistent with a stratospheric intrusion on the cyclonic flank of an upper trough. Across the tropical belt from the eastern Pacific through Central America and into the Caribbean, scattered clusters of bright white deep convective tops are embedded in the broad green moist-air signal, with the most intense cells concentrated over southern Mexico, the Guatemala-Honduras region, and isolated cells over the western Caribbean. No single dominant organized tropical wave or closed circulation is obvious in this frame, though the convective activity over and just east of Central America shows some clustering that could be consistent with a tropical wave passage. The Southern Hemisphere poleward of roughly 40 degrees south shows an active baroclinic zone with elongated cloud bands and red-orange airmass intrusions over the southern cone and adjacent South Atlantic, indicating vigorous westerly wave activity there.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The most striking feature is the 90-100% probability bull's-eye for above-normal temperatures centered on Texas and extending into the southern Plains and Gulf Coast states, indicating the forecasters have very high confidence in a persistent heat signal there. Probability contours step down concentrically outward: the northern and central Plains sit in the 70-80% range, most of the western interior and Southeast in the 60-70% range, and the Pacific Coast and mid-Atlantic corridor in the 33-50% range or near-normal territory. Maine and the immediate Northeast interior are also shaded above-normal at the leaning-above level, while the Great Lakes region is painted near-normal or EC. The only below-normal signal in the contiguous domain is absent entirely; Alaska shows a 60-70% below-normal probability over its interior and western coast, implying a cold upper trough anchored there. The tight, nearly circular gradient of the Texas-centered anomaly, combined with its extreme probability and the lack of any cool signal pushing into the Lower 48, is consistent with a persistent, amplified upper ridge over the south-central U.S. expected to maintain through the August 25-29 window with little indication of the pattern breaking down during this period.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is indeed a CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and height-anomaly forecast, valid 25-29 August 2026. The green solid contours show heights labeled in the 534-594 dam range, and the dashed red and blue contours are anomalies plotted at 6 dam intervals.

The dominant positive anomaly center sits over the interior of western Canada, roughly over the Northwest Territories and northern British Columbia, with values appearing to reach the +9 to +12 dam range based on the dashed red contour spacing. The ridge axis on the height field extends from the northeastern Pacific into central Canada, with the 588 dam contour building well into the continent. A notable negative anomaly center is positioned over the central Canadian Arctic, labeled near -6 dam or lower in blue dashed contours, consistent with the closed low visible in the green height field centered near Baffin Island and surrounding waters. A secondary modest negative anomaly area is suggested over the north-central Pacific and over parts of the eastern U.S. seaboard, where green contours show a broad trough.

Regarding amplification, the zero-anomaly line (boundary between red and blue dashed contours) appears to cross the continent somewhere over the central Plains and Great Lakes region, meaning positive anomalies extend well east of the Rockies but stop short of the eastern seaboard. The western ridge appears to be holding or slightly retrogressing rather than advancing eastward, and the pattern is not trending toward a more zonal configuration given the prominent meridional height gradient between the Arctic low and the western Canadian ridge.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This chart is a 500 mb height and height anomaly (departure from normal) prognostic valid 27 Aug – 02 Sep 2026, made 19 Aug 2026, with heights in dam at 60 dam intervals and anomalies shown by dashed contours in red (positive) and blue (negative).

The dominant feature is a deep closed low centered over the central Canadian Arctic archipelago, with heights near 540 dam at the center; the surrounding height pattern shows strongly amplified cyclonic curvature across the entire northern tier of North America. The anomaly field shows a broad negative center over northern Canada, with contours suggesting departures on the order of –6 to –9 dam in that region, while a modest positive anomaly of roughly +3 to +6 dam is present over the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, where the 594 dam closed high is depicted. There is no meaningful positive height anomaly over western Canada, the northern Rockies, or the northern Plains; instead, the ridge axis has retreated well to the south and southwest, with the ridge core sitting over the Desert Southwest and northern Mexico rather than the northern Rockies — a substantially different and more amplified pattern than a northern-tier ridge outcome. The western portion of the contiguous United States shows heights around 576–582 dam, consistent with a transition zone between the southwestern ridge and the deep Canadian trough to the north, implying a persistent and relatively progressive trough axis somewhere across the central to northern Rockies and northern Plains.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: Heavy rain, flash flooding, and severe weather threat shifts from Ohio/Tennessee Valley this morning to Mid-Atlantic coast today. A convergence zone between stationary and cold fronts will enhance rainfall corridor along I-95 to northern Mid-Atlantic; slight risk excessive rainfall highlighted for today, with damaging winds the main severe threat. Another heavy rain round expected Friday across Carolinas to Mid-Atlantic. Separate severe weather possible today across eastern Nebraska to Minnesota/Wisconsin with large hail threat. Friday severe weather expected in central/eastern Nebraska with potential hail exceeding two inches. Scattered thunderstorms in Southeast pose excessive rainfall risk. Monsoonal activity continues Four Corners region. Dangerous heat persists across South with record highs likely; heat intensifying in Southwest. Extreme Heat Warnings in effect Desert Southwest through Deep South; Heat Advisories for Florida and Southeast coast. Overnight lows in low 80s with high humidity providing minimal relief.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary: Slight risk of severe thunderstorms across the Mid-Atlantic and from the central Plains into the upper Mississippi Valley. Mid-Atlantic: scattered severe storms expected as a shortwave trough and associated surface low move northeast, with damaging wind gusts the primary threat. Supercells and organized lines possible with 40-50 kt shear; couple of tornadoes possible in Delmarva to central New Jersey due to favorable hodographs. Central Plains into upper Mississippi Valley: cold front interacting with moist, unstable air will initiate thunderstorms, expanding southwest from the Upper Mississippi Valley. Large hail (greater than 2 inches) is primary severe hazard in early evening; isolated strong to severe gusts and low-probability tornadoes possible with supercellular mode. Carolinas into Southeast: scattered thunderstorms along cold front with weak shear; strong downbursts possible. Arizona: scattered afternoon/evening storms with lower potential for strong gusts than previous day.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: Severe Thunderstorm Watch 603 covering western and middle Tennessee expires at 11z with no new watch expected. Widespread thunderstorms and stratiform rain continue across the region, but convective intensity has diminished since 09z due to substantial overturning and weakening warm advection. Occasional stronger storms remain possible over the next 1-2 hours near a modestly veering low-level jet, but short-term trends suggest activity will weaken sufficiently to preclude watch replacement. Peak wind gusts up to 60 mph and hail to 1.25 inches remain possible.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
Atlantic: No tropical cyclone formation expected through next 7 days.

East Pacific: Hurricane Lala active southeast of Lisianski Island. Central Pacific area of low pressure east-southeast of Hawaii shows high (90%) formation probability; tropical depression expected to develop today or tonight while moving west-northwestward. Hawaiian Islands should monitor. South of Mexico, tropical wave has low 48-hour (20%) but high 7-day (80%) formation chance, moving offshore. Central East Pacific low pressure shows marginal conditions; 10% 48-hour, 30% 7-day formation probability.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: The Oceanic Niño Index shows a transition from weak La Niña conditions toward neutral and into El Niño. Currently (OND 2025), the index is 26.04°C with a -0.61°C anomaly, indicating La Niña. The anomaly progressively weakens through early 2026, turning positive by February-March. By mid-year 2026, a moderate El Niño is developing, with the anomaly reaching +1.39°C by MJJ 2026. The warming trend accelerates notably from spring onward.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary: PNA weakening into slightly negative territory (latest -0.17, 7-day mean -0.70 after trending down from -0.29). AO rebounded sharply from prior negative phase, now +0.37 on 7-day mean but latest reading dropping to -0.35, suggesting volatility. NAO deteriorating notably, now -0.90 on 7-day mean and -1.28 latest, a substantial swing from prior +0.19. Summer context limits reliability of these extratropical signals individually. The NAO's negative trend is most coherent, favoring Atlantic cutoff persistence; PNA and AO remain transient and warrant corroboration from synoptic features.
